name: GAMMA
tagline: Wisconsin's 1980s shared-nothing parallel database machine that proved hash-partitioned query plans.
description: Gamma was a parallel relational database machine built by David DeWitt's group at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The first prototype ran on 20 VAX 11/750s in 1985 and was ported to a 32-node Intel iPSC/2 hypercube in 1989. It combined three ideas that now underpin every MPP warehouse: shared-nothing nodes with their own disks, horizontal partitioning (declustering) of every relation across those disks, and hash-based parallel joins and aggregates scheduled as dataflow with almost no central coordination. Its published speedup and scaleup measurements became a reference point for the field. Teradata, Greenplum, Redshift and similar systems follow the same blueprint.
statusNote: Research prototype (1984–early 1990s); its shared-nothing, hash-partitioned design lives on in Teradata, Greenplum and other MPP warehouses.

pricing.notes: Never sold or distributed; known through papers.

scale.notes: Ran on up to 32 processors and disks; experiments showed linear speedup for selections and joins.

strengths: Pioneered shared-nothing parallel query execution on commodity processors
Declustered every relation across all disks for parallel scans
Hash-based parallel join and aggregation algorithms without central control
Published speedup and scaleup methodology still used to evaluate MPP systems
weaknesses: Hardware-specific to VAX and iPSC/2 multicomputers
useCases: Background reading before designing an MPP engine
Understanding where partitioned hash joins came from
